Messages.Author: Bob Ellison
Messages.Body:
I just introduced my brother to Jyhad over break; he seems to enjoy it. :-)
One question came up. He used a Rat's Warning to untap a vampire when
a bleed was declared against him. But the untapped vampire did not
block the bleed. Does the vampire remain untapped when the action
is complete? (I thought not, but there's nothing on the card to
refute it...)

That would make an Auspex/Animalism vampire combination interesting;
untap with Rat's Warning in response to a bleed, but then only play
reaction cards (Telepathic Counter), which don't tap you back...

papillo the pongid

Messages.Author: Bob Ellison
Messages.Body:
> Does the vampire remain untapped when the action
> >is complete?

> Absolutely. The card untaps the V. A successful block will tap the V.

I've gotten some private e-mail on this; some say the vampire is tapped,
some don't.

It seems to me that Jyhad is designed so that a vampire that takes
an action, whether complete or blocked, is tapped; such a vampire may
awaken to attempt to block, but always returns to its tapped state at
the completion of the action. This matches the conceptual model that
a vampire taking an action has to spend a lot of time working on it.

There are a few exceptions that are usually clearly noted. Some
powerful cards allow a vampire that is blocked to remain untapped and
free to take further action; this fits with the conceptual model that
the acting vampire didn't have to take as much time to finish the action.
There are some cards that allow blocking vampires to remain untapped
after a block; the explanation is that blocking doesn't require as
much time as a normal action would.

The combinations seem obscure, though. What if a tapped Justine
Wakes with Evening's Freshness and blocks a capacity-3 vampire? Justine
doesn't tap after blocking low-weight vampires, but Wake with Evening's
Freshness taps the vampire after the action. It seems pretty clear
that Justine should end up tapped again; this seems to be the intention
of the ability to untap. This seems to be the case as long as the
actor used Wake, regardless of any other instructions to remain untap
(such as Majesty with superior Presence).

Rat's Warning seems odd. The vampire using it may untap - but may
apparently remain untapped, depending on the interpretation of the
card. It seems to me that if the card intended its wielder to remain
untapped, it would have specifically said so, as such a result is
counter to any other mechanics present in the game. This interpretation
also allows a vampire to take successful actions several times during
one turn of play (consider a Malkavian with an Animalism discipline and
the Madness Network; such a vampire coiuld take successful action after
every players' turn in a multiple-player game). This is also seems
counter to the intent of the rules, which everywhere else enforce
that a vampire may usually only take one attempt at an action, and may
certainly only take one successful action per turn.

If Tom's still around, I'd love to know first whether this use of the
card is a valid interpretation, and second whether it is an interpretation
that was intended by the designers (the two questions are very
different).

papillo the obsequious

> The combinations seem obscure, though. What if a tapped Justine

> doesn't tap after blocking low-weight vampires, but Wake with Evening's
> Freshness taps the vampire after the action. It seems pretty clear

> of the ability to untap. This seems to be the case as long as the
> actor used Wake, regardless of any other instructions to remain untap

Wake with Evening's Freshness does *not* untap the vampire. The vampire
is able to block or play reaction cards *as if* untapped, but he doesn't
physically untap to do it. If you Wake to block a bleed and your predator
plays Lost in Crowds, you've just burned a Wake because your blocker will
not untap in the first place.

Messages.Author: Don Sowell
Messages.Body:
>: They way I view it is the combat itself is what taps the vampire that
>: is blocking. Thus the vampire uses Rat's Warning, thus becomeing
>: untapped. Now it blocks and goes into combat thus becomeing tapped again.

>Actually, it's the blocking that causes the tapping.

What reference says this? For example if I declare my minion, Jing Wei,
is blocking KoKo. You then lay down a Lost in Crowds. Oops, Jing can't
compete. So KoKo goes through and Jing *is not tapped*. But I declared
her as a blocker.

This is, of course, confusing.

What you're saying is that *successful* blocking taps the vampire.
Fair enough. But a successful block, by definition makes the vampires go
into combat. If this is changed (or a counterargument is put forth) I
would change my view, but, IMHO it is easier to think of the combat
itself as tapping the blocking vampire (and the action performed by the
acting minion tapping that vampire).
Especially with the rules team declaring the meta rule that all
combats tap the minions that are involved in that combat (excepting, of
course, specific breaking of this rule).

Don Sowell

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson

>> Yes, the wording on Domain is... interesting. Basically it lets a
>> tapped Prince or Justicar untap and attempt to block at +2 intercept.

Actually,
The wording allows an untapped Prince or Justicar to block at +2
stealth as well:

Prince or Justicar
+2 intercept

Usable by a tapped ...
NOT:
Usable only by a tapped ...

That it *may* be used by a tapped Prince/Justicar is an enhancement to the
function of the card, *not* a limitation.

It's only foolish errata that has gone against logic to require a Prince
or Justicar to be tapped before it can get a bonus to intercept.

I wish the design team would give a reason for this errata.
(Actually I wish they would leave the card alone, but ...)

BledBecauseRakeWasUntapped,

In article <3bghj5$3...@tadpole.fc.hp.com>, pap...@fc.hp.com (Bob Ellison)

> > Does the vampire remain untapped when the action

> awaken to attempt to block, but always returns to its tapped state at
> the completion of the action. This matches the conceptual model that
> a vampire taking an action has to spend a lot of time working on it.
>

First off, blocking and action cause you to tap. Combat does not. This was
according to a net ruling by Tom Wylie.

Second, some "untap" cards (like "Wake with Evening's Freshness") state
that you can untap, but are tapped whether you block successfully or not.

Third, playing reaction cards do not tap you (unless it specifically says
it does, like "Telepathic Misdirection").

"Rat's Warning" is a reaction card playable by a tapped vampire that untaps
you versus a bleed action and does not require you retap at the end of the
action (I believe that is how the card reads). If the predator announces a
bleed, you play R.A. to untap, predator plays stealth to sneak past and you
cannot play any interceptso you play "Telepathic Counter" which reduces the
bleed. You are still untapped. Why? R.A. does not require you to retap and
T.C. is a reaction card and does not require you to tap.

Result: predator's bleeding vamp is tapped, your vamp is untapped, and the
bleed was unsuccessful if it was reduced to 0.

Animalism is tough. There are a lot of ways to use it to stay untapped!

> The combinations seem obscure, though. What if a tapped Justine
> Wakes with Evening's Freshness and blocks a capacity-3 vampire? Justine
> doesn't tap after blocking low-weight vampires, but Wake with Evening's
> Freshness taps the vampire after the action. It seems pretty clear
> that Justine should end up tapped again; this seems to be the intention
> of the ability to untap. This seems to be the case as long as the
> actor used Wake, regardless of any other instructions to remain untap
> (such as Majesty with superior Presence).
>

With a "Wake" she would be tapped because it is not the act of blocking a
lightweight vampire which taps Justine, but the post-"Wake" effect
(otherwise known as PWE). :)=

> Rat's Warning seems odd. The vampire using it may untap - but may
> apparently remain untapped, depending on the interpretation of the
> card. It seems to me that if the card intended its wielder to remain
> untapped, it would have specifically said so, as such a result is
> counter to any other mechanics present in the game.

No, it is the other way around. The mechanics of the game are that when you
untap, you stay untapped until you take an action which causes you to tap.
That is why there is a special note on "Wake" -- because *it* is the card
which breaks the mechanics of the rules; "Rat's Warning" does not.

> This interpretation
> also allows a vampire to take successful actions several times during
> one turn of play (consider a Malkavian with an Animalism discipline and
> the Madness Network; such a vampire coiuld take successful action after
> every players' turn in a multiple-player game). This is also seems
> counter to the intent of the rules, which everywhere else enforce
> that a vampire may usually only take one attempt at an action, and may
> certainly only take one successful action per turn.
>

I once played a deck with 24 (out of 60) "untap"-type cards. It was
maddening to all of the other players, but in the end, it did not win.

> that was intended by the designers (the two questions are very
